section.heading: 6.4. Work
section.paragraph: The term work is used in everyday language to mean the total amount of effort required to perform a task. In physics it has a technical meaning that depends on the idea of a force. Intuitively, you can think of a force as describing a push or pull on an object—for example, a horizontal push of a book across a table or the downward pull of the earth’s gravity on a ball. In general, if an object moves along a straight line with position function $$s(t)$$ , then the force $$F$$ on the object (in the same direction) is given by Newton’s Second Law of Motion as the product of its mass $$m$$ and its acceleration $$a$$ :

In the SI metric system, the mass is measured in kilograms (kg), the displacement in meters (m), the time in seconds (s), and the force in newtons $$(N = {kg} \cdot m \slash s^{2})$$ . Thus a force of $$1$$ N acting on a mass of $$1$$ kg produces an acceleration of $$1m \slash s^{2}$$ . In the US Customary system the fundamental unit is chosen to be the unit of force, which is the pound.
In the case of constant acceleration, the force $$F$$ is also constant and the work done is defined to be the product of the force $$F$$ and the distance $$d$$ that the object moves:

If $$F$$ is measured in newtons and $$d$$ in meters, then the unit for $$W$$ is a newton-meter, which is called a joule (J). If $$F$$ is measured in pounds and $$d$$ in feet, then the unit for $$W$$ is a foot-pound (ft-lb), which is about $$1.36$$ J.

example.heading: Example 1

list.item: (a) How much work is done in lifting a $$1.2$$ -kg book off the floor to put it on a desk that is $$0.7$$ m high? Use the fact that the acceleration due to gravity is $$g = 9.8m \slash s^{2}$$ .
(b) How much work is done in lifting a $$20$$ -lb weight $$6$$ ft off the ground?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The force exerted is equal and opposite to that exerted by gravity, so Equation 1 gives $$F = mg = (1.2)(9.8) = 11.76N$$ and then Equation 2 gives the work done as $$W = Fd = \left( {11.76N} \right)\left( {0.7m} \right) \approx 8.2J$$
(b) Here the force is given as $$F = 20$$ lb, so the work done is $$W = Fd = \left( {20{lb}} \right)\left( {6{ft}} \right) = 120{ft-lb}$$

example.paragraph: Notice that in part (b), unlike part (a), we did not have to multiply by $$g$$ because we were given the weight (which is a force) and not the mass of the object.

section.paragraph: Equation 2 defines work as long as the force is constant, but what happens if the force is variable? Let’s suppose that the object moves along the $$x$$ -axis in the positive direction, from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ , and at each point $$x$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ a force $$f(x)$$ acts on the object, where $$f$$ is a continuous function. We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta x$$ . We choose a sample point $$x_{i}^{*}$$ in the $$i$$ th subinterval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ . Then the force at that point is $$f\left( x_{i}^{*} \right)$$ . If $$n$$ is large, then $$\Delta x$$ is small, and since $$f$$ is continuous, the values of $$f$$ don’t change very much over the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ . example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: When a particle is located a distance $$x$$ feet from the origin, a force of $$x^{2} + 2x$$ pounds acts on it. How much work is done in moving it from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 3$$ ?
Solution
The work done is $$16\frac{2}{3}$$ ft-lb.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: A $$200$$ -lb cable is $$100$$ ft long and hangs vertically from the top of a tall building.

list.item: How much work is required to lift the cable to the top of the building?
How much work is required to pull up only $$20$$ feet of the cable?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: One method is to use an argument similar to the one that led to Definition 4. [For another method, see Exercise 14(b).] Let’s place the origin at the top of the building and the $$x$$ -axis pointing downward as in Figure 2. We divide the cable into small parts with length $$\Delta x$$ . If $$x_{i}^{*}$$ is a point in the $$i$$ th such interval, then all points in the interval are lifted by approximately the same amount, namely $$x_{i}^{*}$$ . The cable weighs $$2$$ pounds per foot, so the weight of the $$i$$ th part is $$\left( 2{lb} \slash {ft})(\Delta x{ft}) = 2\Delta x{lb} \right.$$ . Thus the work done on the $$i$$ th part, in foot-pounds, is $$\underset{force}{\underset{︸}{\left( 2\Delta x \right)}} \cdot \underset{distance}{\underset{︸}{x_{i}^{*}}} = 2x_{i}^{*}\Delta x$$ Figure 2 Details A two-dimensional rendering of a building is drawn alongside a vertical axis labeled x. The positive x axis runs vertically downward and has three tick marks labeled 0, x_i^* and 100, with x_i^8 lying below 0 and 100 lying below x_i^*. The top of the building is directly across x = 0. A cable hangs from the top of the building until directly across x = 100. From the top of the building, a tick cable runs vertically downward until x = 100. The tick mark x_i^*corresponds to a small interval Delta x is marked on the cable. We get the total work done by adding all these approximations and letting the number of parts become large (so $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ ): $$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{2x_{i}^{*}\Delta x = \int_{0}^{100}{2x}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {\left. x^{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{100} = 10,000{ft-lb}}} \end{array}$$ If we had placed the origin at the bottom of the cable and the $$x$$ -axis upward, we would have gotten $$W = \int_{0}^{100}2(100 - x)dx$$ which gives the same answer.

The work required to move the top $$20$$ ft of cable to the top of the building is computed in the same manner as part (a): $$W_{1} = {\int_{0}^{20}{2x}dx = x^{2}\rbrack_{0}^{20}} = 400{ft-lb}$$ Every part of the lower $$80$$ ft of cable moves the same distance, namely $$20$$ ft, so the work done is $$W_{2} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \underset{\underset{distance}{︸}}{20} \cdot \underset{\underset{force}{︸}}{{2\Delta x}} \right) = \int_{20}^{100}40\mathit{dx} = 3200{ft-lb}$$ (Alternatively, we can observe that the lower $$80$$ ft of cable weighs $$80 \cdot 2 = 160{lb}$$ and moves uniformly $$20$$ ft, so the work done is $$160 \cdot 20 = 3200{ft-lb}$$ .) The total work done is $$W_{1} + W_{2} = 400 + 3200 = 3600{ft-lb}$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: A tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with height $$10$$ m and base radius $$4$$ m. It is filled with water to a height of $$8$$ m. Find the work required to empty the tank by pumping all of the water to the top of the tank. (The density of water is $$1000{kg} \slash m^{3}$$ .)

Solution Let’s measure depths from the top of the tank by introducing a vertical coordinate line as in Figure 3. The water extends from a depth of $$2$$ m to a depth of $$10$$ m and so we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {2,10} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and choose $$x_{i}^{*}$$ in the $$i$$ th subinterval. This divides the water into $$n$$ layers. The $$i$$ th layer is approximated by a circular cylinder with radius $$r_{i}$$ and height $$\Delta x$$ . We can compute $$r_{i}$$ from similar triangles, using Figure 4, as follows:

A horizontal line segment of length r_i connects the vertical side and the hypotenuse at a height 10 minus x_i^* from the bottom corner of the triangle.

example.paragraph: Thus an approximation to the volume of the $$i$$ th layer of water is
$$V_{i} \approx \pi r_{i}^{2}\Delta x = \frac{4\pi}{25}\left( {10 - x_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}\Delta x$$
and so its mass is
$$\begin{array}{lcl} m_{i} & = & {{density} \times {volume}} \\ & \approx & {1000 \cdot \frac{4\pi}{25}{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x = 160\pi{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x} \end{array}$$
The force required to raise this layer must overcome the force of gravity and so

Each particle in the layer must travel a distance upward of approximately $$x_{i}^{*}$$ . The work $$W_{i}$$ done to raise this layer to the top is approximately the product of the force $$F_{i}$$ and the distance $$x_{i}^{*}$$ :
$$W_{i} \approx F_{i}x_{i}^{*} \approx 1568\pi x_{i}^{*}\left( {10 - x_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}\Delta x$$
To find the total work done in emptying the entire tank, we add the contributions of each of the $$n$$ layers and then take the limit as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}1568}\pi x_{i}^{*}{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x = \int_{2}^{10}1568}\pi x{({10 - x})}^{2}dx} \\ {\phantom{W} = {1568\pi\int_{2}^{10}{({100x - 20x^{2} + x^{3}})}}dx = 1568\pi\left\lbrack {50x^{2} - \frac{20x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{2}^{10}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {1568\pi\left( \frac{2048}{3} \right) \approx 3.4 \times 10^{6}J}} \end{array}$$
